Reddit had some pretty ridiculous rules regarding the posting of personal content to avoid the label of "spam". The 10:1 ratio was ludicrous. If you want to see a subverse loaded with spam and shit content, tell someone they have to post 9 or 10 links to content that is not their own for every link they post to their own creations. Better yet, show me more than 50 out of the 50000+ users in this subverse who have ever posted more than 10 links to content that is not their own at any point ever.

I was once a part of a subreddit that was devoted to a particular mobile game. I had been taking part in discussions there for a few months without posting any content of my own at all. Given the nature of mobile games, videos of any kind were fairly sparse but there was a lot of fan art (some of which was of the MS Paint 'stick figures drawn with a mouse' variety) and it was never any problem. But as soon as I post a video featuring a review/overview of the game, it's deleted by a mod within a matter of hours. I at first thought it was maybe caught in the automatic spam filter so I messaged the mods to inquire. I was told it was deleted manually because self-promotion was not allowed. I referenced all of the fanart and other content that was submitted daily by their creators. I was pompously informed of how foolish I was to compare their exceptionally talented ART to my crummy video. I responded with a link to the MS Paint mouse drawing from a few days before and asked if that was the kind of "talent" that justified self-promotion of content in the subreddit. I was told that he had found that submission funny, and therefore it was OK.

So it went from "I deleted (censored) your submission because you're not allowed to self-promote your work" to "I deleted the submission because it wasn't up to my standards of talent/quality" to "I deleted your submission because it didn't entertain me."

And that's what it boils down to. It has nothing to do with self promotion. That's just the rationalization. It has everything to do with "I don't personally enjoy them" or "they irritate me." And that is not an adequate justification to exclude self-promoted content.

I could get behind a push to remove self-promoted content with titles that make no real effort to describe the content of the video. It takes longer to determine what a video is about by viewing it than most other forms of media so it makes sense that we would want accurate and meaningful titles to save people a bit of time. If people have their submission removed with a message explaining that the title was too vague, they'll smarten up fairly quickly.

I have certain personal rules and guidelines about how and how often I submit my video content. It boils down to respect for the community and in particular, respect for community members who aren't interested in my content for reasons of their own. They don't want to see daily submissions from me (much less more than one per day) and the people who do enjoy my content don't need me to post every video here in order to be notified when I add a new one to the channel. I make a conscious effort to exercise some restraint and do my part to ease the clutter, and in exchange all I ask is that I be given the same consideration and asked to observe the same rules as any other content creator utilizing any other media format.

In short, singling out video creators for limitations/exclusions is not okay. If someone can post daily links to their own written articles, screenshots, fan art etc., then people should be able to do the same with video content. The rules that apply to one should apply to all or there's something very wrong. There's no justification to try to delineate videos from other types of media aside from personal bias, and personal bias is never an acceptable reason to limit or restrict expression.
